source.title: Truncate or Not? A Scaling Study of Looped Transformers with Truncated Backpropagation
source.authors: Xu-Yuan Xiong; Si-Yu Chen; Zi-Han Shao; Yue Su; Wei-Yang Jin; Ping Luo; Zhuo-Ran Yang; Xi-Hui Liu

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some PDF-extraction artifacts affect symbols and table layout, but the relevant text and results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures loss scaling in looped transformers and refines the scaling form: on its runs, a bounded loop-gain law predicts better than a power-law loop gain. It also tests compute allocation under that fitted law.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own validation-loss scaling experiments, held-out prediction errors, compute allocations, and matched-compute results. Statements about results from prior studies are cited context, not catalog rows. Training-curve panels show training rather than held-out validation loss and are not recorded as validation-loss results.
record.test_reason: The study applies a coupled size–data power law (Videau form) to a new setting: dense prelude–recurrent–coda looped transformers, 58M–919M non-embedding parameters, on FineWeb-Edu. It reports its own in-sample and held-out validation-loss errors, which bear on V1 and V2. It also derives compute-optimal N and D exponents from the fitted law, which bear on V3. Its main contributions concern loop count and truncation. Those axes are not parameters, tokens or compute, so most rows belong under fits_no_version rather than under a version. T3 fits better than T5: the study does not argue that any version is wrong. It extends the size–data law with an effective-parameter term.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Under the fitted law, truncation helps only when the forward-loop count is prescribed; with both counts free, full BPTT is optimal, and matched-compute runs agree. At fixed size, most added compute goes to tokens, with loops growing only about C^0.24. With size free, the law favors no looping. In runs, two fully trained loops come within 0.008 nats with 27–32% fewer parameters and pull ahead with 8% more compute. The authors note the law covers dense models only, measures validation loss only, and fits T up to 16.
record.recipe_differences: Studies prelude–recurrent–coda looped transformers, independently varies forward and backward loop counts, and fits a coupled size–data law with bounded effective-parameter gains. It differs from standard non-looped scaling-law setups and uses a leading-FLOP compute approximation for analytical allocation results.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported conclusions vary with whether forward-loop count is prescribed or jointly optimized, and with loop setting and compute budget. The fitted bounded loop-gain form predicts better than the tested power-law gain form. Analytical allocation depends on the stated FLOP approximation and fixed recurrent-parameter share.

fits_no_version.finding: A bounded loop gain predicts loss better than a power-law gain in loop count: RMSE 8.67e-3 vs 1.65e-2 on loop-setting holdout, and 0.0115 vs 0.0340 at the T=16 holdout. Loss gains saturate with loop count.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In looped transformers, effective parameters from looping saturate rather than growing as a power of loop count.

fits_no_version.finding: More full-BPTT loops lower validation loss at every tested size and budget.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Looping with full BPTT increases effective parameter count in dense looped transformers.

fits_no_version.finding: At a prescribed T, the law selects truncation to B=2 (34% compute saving at T=8). When both loop counts are free, full BPTT wins: (4,4) beats (8,2) at equal compute at all five sizes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Truncated BPTT pays only when the forward-loop count is fixed.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed model size, the law's asymptotic allocation is T*∝C^0.24 and D*∝C^0.76.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute-optimal loop count grows slowly with compute at fixed model size.

fits_no_version.finding: A compute-optimal (2,2) model stays within 0.008 nats of the non-looped model with 27–32% fewer parameters, and beats it with 8% more compute.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Two fully trained loops trade a small compute premium for a large parameter saving.

record.problems: The main grid is dense-only, covers 58M–919M non-embedding parameters and at most 16 forward loops, and measures validation loss rather than downstream performance. The fitted gain ceiling and large-compute allocation rules extend beyond observed loop counts. Compute allocation uses stated approximations; the paper notes that changing parameter proportions or including additional compute terms can affect the simple allocation identities.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying results were left out.

untested.parts: Power-law behaviour over several orders of magnitude in N. The grid spans about 1.2 orders (58M–919M), and fitted budgets span 9–74 tokens per parameter.
Prediction of runs orders of magnitude larger than the fitting runs.
Exponents refit to measured compute-optimal optima across a wide compute range. No direct test of the Kaplan versus Hoffmann split.
Depth, width and other shape choices at a fixed parameter count. Width and depth grow together across sizes.
Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer.
Downstream task performance. The study measures validation loss only.
How parameter counting, schedule, data or fitting method change the N/D exponents or the compute-optimal split.

missing.what: Law RMSE on configurations outside the fitted tokens-per-parameter range: 0.0200, versus 0.0031–0.0093 on fitted configurations, and 0.0148 versus 0.0053 for full-BPTT settings.
The law places the non-looped compute-optimal model at a larger size than the measured IsoFLOP runs.
The largest-size holdout fit reaches the E=0 bound. Max errors per holdout run 2.04e-2 to 2.63e-2.
The non-looped (T=1) row holdout gives RMSE 0.0172, the weakest boundary check.

record.verdict_notes: Most rows concern the loop and truncation axes, which no version names; I moved them to fits_no_version. V1–V3 evidence rests on the size–data component of the law over a narrow scale range (about 1.2 orders in N). The V3 exponents are analytic consequences of the fit, not measured optima. The training-curve frontier (Fig. 4) uses training loss and was rightly left out.

versions.untested_parts: Tests validation loss scaling for dense looped transformers using a coupled size–data law and an effective-parameter loop term. Does not separately establish the original simple power laws for standard non-looped models in every non-bottleneck regime or over orders of magnitude beyond its tested range.
Tests held-out configurations, sizes, token budgets, and loop settings within the study's experimental grid; does not test predictions orders of magnitude beyond the sampled sizes or budgets.

Tests compute allocation within its fitted law and compute approximation, including fixed-size loop/token allocation and free-size parameter/token allocation. Does not establish a universal allocation trend across architectures or compute-counting choices.
The study does not systematically vary depth, width, or architecture details at fixed parameter count to test their effect on loss.
No other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer regimes are tested.
The study measures validation loss, not downstream task performance or reasoning ability.

Directly compares bounded and power-law loop-gain forms on this setup. It does not systematically vary parameter-count conventions, datasets, training schedules, or fitting methods to measure how those choices change the exponents or compute-optimal split.
